newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN GRAIN - WHEAT GETS RAIN, AWB FEELS HEAT.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN GRAIN - WHEAT GETS RAIN, AWB FEELS HEAT.

text.p: Australia's threatened 1997/98 wheat crop last week received its first reasonable rain in southern and eastern parts of the grainsbelt in months.
This followed further severe downgradings of the current season's wheat crop, but was not seen by forecasters and analysts as enough to boost the size of the estimated crop.
Physical markets were quiet as futures prices gyrated, finally closing on Friday slightly higher over the week.

While markets waited for rain and for clearer signs of where the crop was headed, domestic politics in the Australian grains industry became increasingly intense. The Australian Wheat Board (AWB) was almost as much of a focus as the crop itself.
Deadlines set for Australian grains growers to agree to a new share structure for the privatising AWB passed by without agreement, with the main split between Western Australian growers and the rest.
By week's end the Western Australian Farmers Federation said it may ask the federal governent to divide the board's export monopoly into two, one for eastern states and one for the west.
Western Australian objections to the proposed new corporate structure centre on how shares in the privatised body will be allocated, as well as on taxation issues.
But the row is seen by the AWB's opponents, including major international grains traders, as a possible first crack in the AWB's export monopoly wall.
Regional meetings on the issue will continue this week.

Big world grains traders, through the Australian Grain Exporters Association (AGEA), on Friday also entered the domestic debate, accusing Australia's Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer of showing signs of belief that an Australian government competition review of the AWB's monopoly export powers might be a foregone conclusion -- with the monopoly to be maintained.

AGEA, whose members include local offshoots of Cargill, Continental Grain and other major world players, said it had written to Fischer over the issue, rejecting an insinuation that they would exploit small growers if they were not protected by statutory marketing authorities such as the AWB.

Meanwhile, rain fell across widespread areas of South Australia, Victoria and New South Wales (NSW) in the second part of last week, raising hopes that Australia will produce an average crop for the season.
Wheat prices rose over the week under the conflicting influence of big cuts in crop forecasts, higher AWB pool prices and the rain which fell later in the week.
Sydney Futures Exchange wheat contracts first reacted cautiously to the rain, initially falling then rising on Thursday on fears that the rain was not enough to save the crop.
Continued rainfall into Friday, however, pushed SFE wheat prices down as the market became convinced that sufficient rain had fallen to ensure the crop's survival, for the time being.
Rainfall figures in the three days to Friday showed about one inch falling in wheatgrowing areas in South Australia, Victoria and NSW. Analysts say more rain is needed.
This followed crop downgradings during the week by both the AWB and private forecaster, Australian Wheat Forecasters Pty Ltd (AWF).

The AWB cut its forecast crop size by one million tonnes to a 14 million to 15 million tonne range, while AWF chopped its forecast to 15.3 million tonnes from its month-earlier forecast of 17.87 million tonnes.
Crop estimates were not likely to rise because of the rain which had fallen during the week, AWB crop forecaster Michael Shean said on Friday.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
